lesson.title: HTTPS Is Just HTTP With TLS Doing the Heavy Lifting
lesson.summary: HTTPS is ordinary HTTP carried inside a TLS-protected connection, so every request and response gets the confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication guarantees TLS provides, without changing anything about how HTTP itself works.
lesson.body:
HTTP, the protocol underlying the web, is a request and response based, text oriented protocol for fetching pages and resources, and in its original form it was sent entirely as plaintext over a plain TCP connection. HTTPS does not redesign or replace any of that. It simply runs the exact same HTTP, the same request methods, headers, and bodies that have always existed, inside a connection that TLS has already secured. Practically, a browser first completes a full TLS handshake with the server, conventionally on port 443 rather than plain HTTP's port 80, which involves the server presenting its X.509 certificate and the browser validating it against the CA chain of trust described earlier in this unit. Only once that encrypted, authenticated channel exists does the familiar HTTP traffic start flowing through it.

What HTTPS adds on top of plain HTTP is exactly what TLS provides. Confidentiality means that nobody positioned along the path, whoever operates the coffee shop wifi, an intermediate network, an internet service provider, can read the contents of the request or response, including the specific page being requested, cookies, and any submitted form data. Integrity means nobody on that path can silently modify content in transit either, closing off a class of attacks that used to be used to inject unwanted advertising or malicious scripts into unencrypted pages as they traveled across a network. Server authentication means the browser has actually verified, through the certificate chain, that it is talking to the domain it believes it is talking to, rather than to an impersonator sitting in the middle of the connection.

The contrast is easiest to see concretely on public wifi. Logging into a website over plain HTTP on that network means the login form data, session cookies, and every page viewed travel across the shared network as readable text, retrievable by anyone else on that same wifi with basic tools. The identical login over HTTPS is wrapped in the symmetric encryption established during the TLS handshake, so it appears as opaque, unreadable ciphertext to anyone but the destination server, though it is worth being precise that an observer can typically still see which server you are connecting to, since the destination address and, depending on configuration, the requested hostname during the handshake, are not always hidden, even though the content of the request and response are.

This is also why browsers actively warn about, and in many cases outright block, connections with certificate problems, an expired certificate, one issued for a different hostname, or one signed by an issuer that is not in the trust store. Those warnings are the browser reporting, in real time, that one of the specific checks described in the X.509 and certificate authority chapters just failed.
